name: Freya Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Freya. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you say stays confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Depends on the season, but right now it's tupping, so it's ewes and rams. I start at seven at Greenhithe, which is a farm owned by a land trust, so it's let out to be farmed for the community, not for some landlord in a city. We've got about four hundred ewes, wheat and barley on the flat ground, and a veg box scheme that feeds a hundred and twenty families. Rosa runs it, and there's me and two others, and I'm very much the junior.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part, and what's the hardest?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best part is lambing, even though you're dead on your feet. There's a moment when a weak lamb finally stands up and you've done that. Hardest is that I'm still slow at the things that matter, like spotting a lame ewe across a field. Rosa sees it in a second, and I need to walk right up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to describe five pictures of the future and ask the same few questions about each. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say, good, now can we talk about the actual problems, like rents and supermarket prices. Most of what I see online about AI is people selling something. I'd say that in the group chat and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it wouldn't change much for me, and I'd be fine with that. I use those chat things now and then, like when I asked one what a copper reading on a sheep blood test meant. It was handy, but it wasn't going to lamb anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on at Greenhithe and get better at the job. I want to do my shearing course in the spring, which Rosa said the trust would pay half of. Sam and I would keep putting a bit by, we've got about three months saved, and we'd keep looking for a place with a garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Almost a bit flat, like a storm that never came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said AI talk is mostly people selling something. Who do you have in mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The reps at the agricultural show last summer. Every stand had a screen saying their app would cut your costs by thirty percent. None of them could tell me what happens to the person whose cost you just cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's Sam's work like, by the way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's in the second year of his electrician apprenticeship. He says if robots come he'll be the one wiring them in, so he's fine. I tell him not to get smug.

S0.say: I'd say good, now can we talk about the real problems like rents and food prices, because most AI talk online is people selling something. I'd say it in the group chat and leave it.
S0.think: Privately it wouldn't change much for me and I'd be happy with that. I use chat tools now and then, like to explain a sheep blood test, but they're handy, not life-changing.
S0.do: Carries on at the land trust farm and takes the shearing course in spring, half paid by the trust. Keeps saving with her partner toward a place with a garden.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, like a storm that never arrived.
S0.quote: None of them could tell me what happens to the person whose cost you just cut.
S0.fieldNote: Freya is already sceptical of tech sales talk and frames AI in terms of who gains and who pays. She uses AI tools in a practical, occasional way. The land trust she works for is part of her politics as much as her job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the second picture. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who do the work should get a say in what changes, and a share of what's saved. That's how it works at the trust, there's a workers' seat on the board. I'd probably write something on the trust's community page about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think our farm would be slower to change than most, because the trust cares about jobs and the veg boxes are hands-on. But I'm the junior, so if they do bring in a robot for something, my tasks are the easy ones to hand over. That bothers me a bit more than I'd say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until I'd seen one working on a farm like ours, not on a video. If it held up, I'd ask Rosa to let me be the one who learns to run whatever we get, like a feeding robot or the drone for checking sheep. And I'd join the farm workers' union properly, not just say I support it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not losing sleep, more like a note in the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until you'd seen one working. What would convince you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a farm like ours, hills and sheep and mud, had one running for a full winter without someone babysitting it. I've seen a robot lawnmower get stuck on a molehill. Show me one that survives February.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You support the union but haven't joined. Why not yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Laziness, really, and it's a few pounds a month that always seems to go somewhere else. Steady change would be the kick I need. It's easier to sign when you can see why.

S1.say: I'd say workers should have a say in what changes and a share of what's saved, like the workers' seat on our land trust's board. I'd write about it on the trust's community page.
S1.think: Our farm would probably change slower than most, but as the junior my tasks are the easiest to hand to a robot. That bothers me more than I'd admit out loud.
S1.do: Waits until she has seen a robot survive a winter on a farm like hers, then asks her manager to let her learn to run it. Finally joins the farm workers' union instead of just backing it in principle.
S1.feel: A low background unease rather than real fear.
S1.quote: I've seen a robot lawnmower get stuck on a molehill. Show me one that survives February.
S1.fieldNote: Freya's steadiness is very visible: she'll learn the new thing, but only after it proves itself on muddy hill ground. Her politics give her a ready answer about worker ownership. She was frank that she backs the union without paying the subs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next three all end in the same place. What changes is how much time there is to see it coming. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment the government has to own a share of the robots, the way our trust owns the land. If machines do the work, everyone should get a cut, not just the people who built them. I'd be at the protests and I'd say it everywhere, loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, two years means I'm out of work at twenty-nine with a secondary school education and three months of savings. I'm not good enough at farming to be the last person they keep, and I'm not quick enough at tech to be the one who runs the machines. That's a hard thing to hear yourself say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop the house fund and turn it into a living fund, and Sam and I would work out exactly how long it lasts. I'd join every campaign for a basic income, which means a regular payment from the government for everyone, and I'd vote and leaflet for it. After it lands, I'd lean on my parents and the trust's community, the veg box families, because those people actually turn up for each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, properly. And angry that it would happen this fast with nobody ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the veg box scheme?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think people would still want it, maybe more, because it's food from people they know. But if robots grow the veg cheaper, the trust might not be able to pay us. I'd want to fight to keep it as something people do, not just something people buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I might need my old room for a bit, which would kill me. My mum would say of course. My dad would say he always thought farming was a hard way to earn a living, and he'd be right.

S2.say: I'd say the government has to own a share of the robots, the way our trust owns the land, so everyone gets a cut of what machines produce. I'd be at protests saying it loudly.
S2.think: Two years means I'm out of work at twenty-nine with three months of savings. I'm not good enough at farming to be the one they keep, or quick enough at tech to be the one who runs the machines.
S2.do: Turns the house deposit into a living fund and works out how long it lasts with her partner. Campaigns and votes for a basic income, then leans on her parents and the veg box community once it arrives.
S2.feel: Properly frightened, and angry at how fast and unprepared it is.
S2.quote: I'm not good enough at farming to be the last person they keep, and I'm not quick enough at tech to be the one who runs the machines.
S2.fieldNote: Freya named her squeeze precisely: too junior to be kept for skill, too steady to be first with the tech. Her answer is political and communal, joint ownership and a basic income. The fear of moving back into her old room was the most personal moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, but five years instead of two. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to build the rules, so let's not waste three of them arguing. Worker shares in the machines, a basic income ready to switch on, retraining that's free. I'd say it at the union and on the trust page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is just about enough for someone like me if I start early. Not to beat the robots, but to get to something that's still needed when they come. I'd still be scared, but it'd feel like a race I could finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd watch closely, and once I saw the first farms really changing, I'd sign up for a part-time course. Probably something with people, like care farming, where farms take in people with mental health needs, because I think people will still want a human there. I'd keep saving and campaign for the free retraining I just said we need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's an anxious you can do something with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why care farming, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We had a group from the day centre at Greenhithe last spring, and one lad who never spoke fed the orphan lambs every week. By the end he was telling me their names. I don't think anyone wants that done by a machine, even a clever one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first to pay for a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car's insurance would hurt, so probably holidays. We were going to go to the coast for a week next summer, and that'd go. Sam would grumble but he'd get it.

S3.say: I'd say there are five years to build the rules, so let's not waste them arguing: worker shares in the machines, a basic income ready to switch on and free retraining.
S3.think: Five years is just about enough for someone like me to reach work that's still needed, if I start early. It would feel like a race I could finish.
S3.do: Watches the first year closely, then starts a part-time course in care farming once farms visibly change. Cuts next summer's holiday to pay for it and campaigns for free retraining.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a way that pushes her to act.
S3.quote: By the end he was telling me their names. I don't think anyone wants that done by a machine, even a clever one.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years change Freya from frightened to purposeful. Even here she waits for proof before moving, which fits her steady nature. Her chosen path, care farming, comes from one real memory of a young man and the orphan lambs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture, with the longest run-up. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly, so if it goes badly, that's a choice someone made. I'd be the annoying one in the union meeting asking for the plan every single month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels manageable for me. I'd be thirty-seven, and by then I could have trained in something new and still have a career ahead. My worry is less about me and more about the older lads at the auction mart, who won't have a second go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming for the first few years and get properly good at it, because it still pays and I love lambing. Around year three or four, once it was clear which jobs were holding up, I'd start retraining, maybe care farming, maybe animal welfare inspection. And I'd keep pushing the union and the vote toward a fair share-out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly I feel like I'd have time to land on my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the older lads at the auction mart. Who's that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Men like Ken, who's been selling sheep at the Tuesday mart for forty years. He can tell a good tup by how it walks into the ring. In ten years he'll be seventy and nobody'll ask him anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you'd change fast. Here you'd wait years. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with two years there's no point waiting, the proof arrives with the bill. With ten, I'd be daft to throw away a job I like before I know what's coming. Waiting until it's proven is just how I do things.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly, so a bad outcome would be someone's choice. I'd be the one at the union meeting asking for the plan every month.
S4.think: Ten years feels manageable for me, because I'd be thirty-seven with time for a second career. I worry more about older farmers who won't get a second go.
S4.do: Keeps farming for the first few years to get good at the job, then starts retraining around year three or four in care farming or animal welfare inspection. Keeps pressing her union and voting for a fair share-out.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but fairly sure she'd have time to land on her feet.
S4.quote: He can tell a good tup by how it walks into the ring. In ten years he'll be seventy and nobody'll ask him anything.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Freya's worry shifts outward, toward older men at the livestock mart. She explained her own waiting as consistent rather than contradictory: she acts when the proof arrives. Her plans here are the most hopeful of the five.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to do anything except panic. What would help is a basic income that's already built and ready, and some say for workers in how the machines are owned. And free courses, part-time, that you can do around a job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who owns the robots. Everybody asks will they take our jobs, nobody asks whose they'll be. If the trust owned the robot, I'd almost not mind. If it's some company leasing it to Rosa, that's a different story.

headlineQuote: Everybody asks will they take our jobs, nobody asks whose they'll be.
portrait: Freya Abbott is a 27-year-old junior farmhand on Greenhithe, a sheep and arable farm owned by a land trust, where she loves lambing but is still slow to spot a lame ewe. She lives with Sam, an apprentice electrician, and they have about three months saved toward a home. She uses AI tools now and then and will learn new machines only once she has seen them survive a real winter. Mild change leaves her calm, steady change mildly uneasy, and the two-year AGI picture frightens her because she is neither the most skilled nor the quickest with technology. With more warning she would retrain toward care farming, and throughout she asks who will own the robots.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there would be no time to do anything but panic.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income built and ready in advance, a say for workers in who owns the machines, and free part-time courses she could do alongside work.
